articles.title: Scaling Actors and Workers With HPA In Agent Substrate
articles.description: The number one rule of scaling is ensuring that you have more than enough resources readily available...
articles.body_html:
The number one rule of scaling is ensuring that you have more than enough resources readily available to consume, digest, and schedule what you need to run. In the case of agentic workloads, that's typically Agents. For example, is there enough memory to run multi-Actor Workers? Or do you need to scale Workers out to schedule Actors accordingly?

In this blog post, you'll learn how to schedule and scale Actors (where Agents run) via Workers and WorkerPools for any number of Actors that need to run within your environment.

Prerequisites

To follow along with this blog post from a hands-on perspective, you will need:

  1. A cluster with Agent Substrate running (e.g., GKE or a local cluster like Kind).
    1. Agentgateway set as the dataplane proxy for your atenet-router.
  2. Worker images built with your underlying isolation layer (e.g., gVisor).
    1. You can build these images via the Agent Substrate repo (you need to clone it down) ./hack/run-tool.sh and see how to do it here.

What Will You Be Deploying?

Going through this blog post, you will be:

  1. Deploying Actors
  2. "Parking" an Actor until a Worker is ready to schedule it.
  3. Scaling out Workers so if you have, let's say 3 Actors but only 2 Workers, HPA can scale out the Worker (a Pod) to schedule the third Actor.

The goal here is to park Actors when there aren't enough Workers, or memory in the Workers, readily available to schedule an Actor. The Workers in this blog have a 1Gi memory limit, and each Actor asks for 768Mi. A second Actor needs 1536Mi, which means it won't fit. If anyone raises the WorkerPool memory or lowers the Template's, Actors will start sharing workers. Once a Worker is made available, the Actor can be automatically scheduled on said Worker so your Agent can run.

To go through the hands-on portion of this blog post in the way that it is configured, you'll want to clone this repo as it has all of the scripts and HPA configurations to run the lab along with Step 1 and Step 2, which is building the images and deploying your Workers.

Deploying Actors

The first step is deploying Actors. All Actors, when deployed, are automatically in a "suspended" state. Because they're in a suspended state, they aren't technically running, which is where the efficiency and overall performance of Agent Substrate come into play. Actors are only running when there is an active session to said Actor. That way, they aren't consuming resources (CPU/memory) for no reason.

Actors sit in a "warm state", which means they don't take seconds to resume. That way, when you create a session to an Actor that's running an Agent, it won't feel like the Actor is in a cold state and takes forever to resume/respond to the request that you're sending to the Actor running an Agent.

  1. Deploy the Actors. The pool caps each worker at 1Gi of memory (manifests/workerpool.yaml.tmpl), and the template asks for 768Mi per actor (manifests/actortemplate.yaml.tmpl). The scheduler only places an actor where its memory still fits, so a second actor never does. 
for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do
  kubectl ate create actor "a$i" -a ate-lab-burst --template burst
done

💡

the burst template is what's created in actortemplate.yaml.tmpl.

All six start in ACTOR_STATE_SUSPENDED. They exist only as records, plus the golden snapshot in GCS.

  1. Confirm that the Actors are in a suspended state and in Agent Substrate. 
kubectl get actors -a ate-lab-burst

You should see an output similar to the screenshot below.

As you're going through the rest of this blog post, an important note to keep in mind is that because six Actors were deployed and there are two Workers, there's a 3:1 ratio here. That means two Actors can be scheduled, but four cannot and therefore sit in a "parked" state until a Worker is available.

Park and Schedule An Actor

With the Actors deployed, let's resume two of the Actors, and then try a third, which will sit in a parked state until a Worker becomes readily available.

  1. Port-forward the router so it's open and accepting requests (for when a client or something like curl needs to reach it). 
kubectl -n ate-system port-forward svc/atenet-router 8000:80
  1. Fill both Workers with Actors. 
curl -s -H "ate-target-actor: ate-lab-burst/a1" http://localhost:8000
curl -s -H "ate-target-actor: ate-lab-burst/a2" http://localhost:8000
  1. Check and confirm that both Workers got assigned an Actor. 
kubectl ate get workers -n ate-lab-burst

You'll see an output similar to the below:

NAME                                   POOL    STATE                 ACTORS   CPU      MEMORY      POD                                    AGE
cc852e96-6035-47a1-96e9-1b85d2b47c95   burst   WORKER_STATE_ACTIVE   1/1000   0/500m   768Mi/1Gi   ate-lab-burst/burst-6ff589448f-t26t7   20m
43210b1e-2a85-496c-96e9-497575d4e200   burst   WORKER_STATE_ACTIVE   1/1000   0/500m   768Mi/1Gi   ate-lab-burst/burst-6ff589448f-t7gm6   20m
  1. Try assigning a third Actor. 
curl -s -w '-> HTTP %{http_code} in %{time_total}s\n' \
  -H "ate-target-actor: ate-lab-burst/a3" http://localhost:8000

You'll get a "request timed out" with a 504. The reason why is that there isn't enough memory on either Worker to schedule the third Actor.

  1. Suspend Actor 1 and then run the curl again. 
kubectl ate suspend actor a1 -a ate-lab-burst

curl -s -w '-> HTTP %{http_code} in %{time_total}s\n' \
  -H "ate-target-actor: ate-lab-burst/a3" http://localhost:8000

You'll see that Actor 3 can now be scheduled.

Add HPA For WorkerPools

In the previous section, you saw that because there are two Workers available within the WorkerPool, only 2/3 of the Actors could be scheduled on the Worker until a Worker freed up.

As you read in the What Will You Be Deploying? section, multiple Actors CAN be scheduled on one Worker as long as there's enough memory to support it. The scenario we want HPA for WorkerPools is when the Worker runs out of memory and therefore a new Worker (Pod/replica) needs to be created.

Tldr; Where HPA comes into play is scaling out an Actor to another Worker (or as many Workers as are needed based on how many Actors are waiting to be unparked).

💡 Because you created six Actors in the Deploying Actors section and the HPA config allows up to 10 replicas, all six Actors will be deployed onto the Workers as there will now be more Workers available because the replica count in the HPA config goes up to ten.

  1. Use the burst script to wake up all six Actors 
./scripts/burst.sh -m hold -d 120

You'll see 504s (timeouts) for the 4 Actors that aren't scheduled on Workers as they aren't scheduled and therefore, aren't running.

  1. In another terminal, scale your WorkerPool to 6 replicas 
kubectl -n ate-lab-burst scale workerpool burst --replicas=6
  1. Go back to the first terminal and you'll see the scale start to occur (from 2/2 to 6/6). This shows that all six Actors are now up and running with successful 200's.

This proves out that scaling the Workers officially worked!

Wrapping Up

Scale becomes increasingly important in the world of agentic because it impacts so many areas. It's not just one app that impacts a department or a particular functionality of an app that impacts a customer. If an Agent is down, it can potentially impact the entire organization. That's why ensuring that scale can be properly implemented across Agents isn't just about the tech teams; it's everyone from engineering to marketing to HR and all teams that are incorporating AI into daily workflows.

articles.title: Stop Guessing. Let the Algorithm Find the Sweet Spot.
articles.description: A reproducible Rust experiment in simulated annealing, search budgets, and the engineering discipline of measuring what matters.
articles.body_html:
Simulated annealing gives a search permission to get worse before it gets better. The useful part is learning when that permission pays off.

There is a familiar ritual in software engineering: increase the thread count, change the batch size, run the benchmark, and squint at the result. Then change another number.

Eventually, something looks better, and we call it optimized.

But better than the previous attempt is a low bar. How much of the search space did we explore? What did each experiment cost? Does the improvement survive a different workload?

Those questions are the difference between tuning by habit and running an optimization experiment.

Simulated annealing is one way to run that experiment. Its most interesting feature is also its least intuitive: sometimes it accepts a worse candidate on purpose.

Let's examine why, implement the rule in Rust, and compare it with greedy search, random search, and a grid. Every method gets the same evaluation budget. The experiment is small enough to run locally and check exhaustively.

Why the first valley can trap you

Imagine walking through a mountain range at night, trying to find its lowest point. You can see nearby terrain, so you keep taking downhill steps.

Eventually, every nearby step leads uphill. You have found a local minimum. Another valley might be deeper, but your rule prevents you from crossing the ridge.

That is the problem with accepting only immediate improvements. Whether a solution is a local minimum also depends on the moves your search permits. A larger jump might cross a barrier that a small step cannot.

Simulated annealing sometimes accepts uphill moves. It borrows its name from the connection between cooling physical materials and searching for low-energy configurations, developed in Kirkpatrick, Gelatt, and Vecchi's 1983 paper.

In the algorithm, energy becomes an objective score. Temperature becomes a parameter controlling the willingness to accept regressions. Cooling gradually reduces that willingness.

This creates a route out of some local minima. A finite run can still miss the best solution.

The acceptance rule

Suppose lower scores are better. Calculate the change from the current candidate:

delta = score(candidate) - score(current)

Accept improvements and ties. For a worse candidate, draw a uniform random number between zero inclusive and one exclusive, then accept when it is smaller than:

p = exp(-delta / temperature)

This is the usual Metropolis acceptance rule for symmetric proposals, used in the original simulated annealing paper. Symmetric means the chance of proposing a move equals the chance of proposing its reverse.

For a regression of two score units, the probability is about 82% at temperature 10, 14% at temperature 1, and effectively zero at temperature 0.1.

Temperature has the same units as the score. Multiply every score by 1,000 and keep the old temperature, and you have changed the search's behavior. A cooling schedule is a design choice, not a magic constant.

Also keep two records: where the search is now and the best candidate it has ever found. Exploring a worse configuration should not erase a better answer.

Define what good means before searching

Consider these hypothetical service settings:

Setting Allowed values Count
Worker threads Every integer from 1 to 64 64
Batch size Every integer from 32 to 4,096 4,065
Timeout 50 to 2,000 milliseconds, stepping by 10 196

That is 50,991,360 configurations. At one evaluation per second, sequential exhaustive search would take about 590 days, before repeats or setup costs.

The hard part starts before choosing a search algorithm. What makes a configuration good?

One possible objective is:

score = 0.5 * (p99_latency / reference_latency)
      + 0.3 * (memory / reference_memory)
      - 0.2 * (throughput / reference_throughput)

Fix those positive reference values before the experiment. The ratios are dimensionless; the weights express your priorities. Changing the scales during the search would make scores from different iterations incomparable.

Hard requirements need separate treatment. If a configuration violates a memory cap, correctness invariant, or latency limit, reject it as infeasible. A throughput gain should not quietly compensate for breaking a requirement.

Even among feasible candidates, there may be several reasonable trade-offs. A candidate lies on the Pareto frontier if no feasible alternative improves an objective without worsening another. A weighted score expresses a preference among trade-offs; it does not discover your priorities for you.

The most important function is the one that decides what good looks like.

Give the algorithm something we can verify

For an executable demonstration, use a smaller problem where we can check the answer exhaustively.

The companion Rust project searches a 64 by 64 grid of abstract parameter indices. Each index maps onto a coordinate between -5.12 and 5.12. Its objective is the two-dimensional Rastrigin function:

E(x, y) = x*x + y*y + 20
        - 10*cos(2*pi*x) - 10*cos(2*pi*y)

The quadratic terms pull the search toward the center. The cosine terms add many local valleys. These scores have no latency, throughput, or dollar units. This is a deterministic mathematical experiment.

The continuous function reaches zero at the origin. Our even-sized grid does not contain the origin, so we enumerate all 4,096 grid points to find the discrete optimum. That enumeration is a separate reference calculation, unavailable to the search algorithms.

The comparison fixes these choices before running:

  • 256 objective evaluations per run, including the initial candidate and repeated proposals.
  • The same initial point, index (63, 63), for each method.
  • 30 seeds, numbered 1 through 30, for the stochastic methods.
  • Annealing and greedy search share a neighborhood: move one index by a signed step of 1 through 8. An out-of-range proposal stays in place and still costs an evaluation.
  • Annealing cools geometrically from 20 to 0.1 over its 255 proposals. Greedy search accepts only improvements or ties.
  • Random search samples the whole grid with replacement. Grid search uses a fixed 16 by 16 subset, rounding evenly spaced coordinates to integer indices.

Equal evaluation counts make one cost comparable. They do not give all methods identical information or movement rules. The starting point, neighborhood, grid spacing, and cooling schedule remain consequential choices.

The Rust loop

The project has no external Rust dependencies. Its seeded generator makes the search repeatable on the tested toolchain. This is the loop from the implementation; validation, random generation, and candidate construction live in the companion source.

/// Minimize an objective while retaining the best state ever visited.
pub fn anneal<S: Clone>(
    initial: S,
    mut score: impl FnMut(&S) -> f64,
    mut neighbor: impl FnMut(&S, &mut Rng) -> S,
    seed: u64,
    schedule: Schedule,
) -> Result<Outcome<S>, String> {
    schedule.validate()?;
    let mut rng = Rng::new(seed)?;
    let mut current = initial;
    let mut current_score = finite(score(&current))?;
    let mut result = Outcome {
        best: current.clone(),
        best_score: current_score,
        evaluations: 1,
        accepted_uphill: 0,
    };

    for proposal in 0..schedule.evaluations - 1 {
        let candidate = neighbor(&current, &mut rng);
        let candidate_score = finite(score(&candidate))?;
        result.evaluations += 1;
        let delta = finite(candidate_score - current_score)?;
        let temperature = schedule.temperature(proposal);
        if delta <= 0.0 || rng.unit() < (-delta / temperature).exp() {
            result.accepted_uphill += usize::from(delta > 0.0);
            current = candidate;
            current_score = candidate_score;
            if current_score < result.best_score {
                result.best = current.clone();
                result.best_score = current_score;
            }
        }
    }
    Ok(result)
}

The boundary handling matters. We choose signed moves with equal probability and leave invalid moves at the current point. Simply clamping an arbitrary move to the nearest boundary would accumulate probability there and lose the symmetry assumed by this acceptance rule.

The implementation also rejects invalid settings and nonfinite objective values, counts evaluations explicitly, and tests that a temporarily worse current state cannot overwrite the best result.

A separate unit test makes the barrier explicit: three adjacent states have costs 1, 2, 0. Starting at the first state, greedy search cannot cross the middle state. With the test's fixed seed and temperature, annealing accepts the uphill move and then reaches zero. That tiny fixture verifies the mechanism; it is not evidence that annealing usually wins.

Run it and compare the evidence

The companion project includes the Rust source, raw results, an independent results checker, and a plotting script. Clone it and run:

git clone https://github.com/copyleftdev/simulated-annealing-article.git
cd simulated-annealing-article
export CARGO_TARGET_DIR=target
cargo test --locked
cargo run --release --locked -- results/raw.csv
python3 scripts/verify.py --reproduce
python3 scripts/analyze.py

Python analysis uses the standard library. Add Matplotlib to regenerate the figures with python3 scripts/analyze.py --plots.

Method Median best score Best to worst score Exact grid optimum hits
Annealing 2.565 2.565 to 2.565 30/30
Greedy 2.565 2.565 to 2.565 30/30
Random 4.220 2.565 to 8.425 5/30
Coarse grid 3.480 3.480 to 3.480 No (deterministic)

Lower is better. The exhaustive grid optimum is 2.564508, and both annealing and greedy search reached it in all 30 runs. Annealing accepted between 14 and 33 uphill moves per run, but those moves did not improve its final score over greedy search here.

That result is a useful correction to the valley metaphor. Our neighborhood allows jumps of up to eight index positions. The cosine ripples repeat roughly every six positions, so greedy search can jump across hills without accepting a worse landing point. This experiment gives us no reason to prefer annealing over this greedy baseline on final score.

Random search reached the optimum in five runs. The coarse grid returned the same result every time; repeating it creates no new statistical evidence. Its chosen spacing misses the central indices 31 and 32, so its result is sensitive to grid alignment. These are observed score ranges, not confidence intervals or a universal ranking.

The raw CSV also records search duration. With such a cheap objective, optimizer overhead and machine conditions can substantially affect timing. An evaluation count is not a measurement of infrastructure savings.

There is a second check: after each run selects its best candidate, the harness shifts each coordinate by either -0.1 or +0.1, evaluates all four combinations, and records their mean score. These four evaluations are outside the 256-call search budget and its timer, and the search never sees their scores. This tests sensitivity to a small, specified change in the formula. It does not simulate production traffic or establish robustness to measurement noise.

That distinction matters. Thirty seeds describe variation in search outcomes on one fixed problem. They are not thirty independent workloads.

Try breaking the optimizer

A passing test suite deserves a challenge too. We used cargo-mutants to alter the library and rerun its tests. The original eight Rust tests missed 53 of 181 generated mutations, including deleting the minus sign in the acceptance formula.

After adding acceptance and contract tests, 153 mutations triggered test failures. Two survived: they permute symmetric terms in the shifted-score average, preserving its mathematical value. Another 25 did not compile, and one caused a nonterminating loop detected by a timeout. We report those categories separately in the mutation review.

The statistical check drives the real kernel through one million uphill proposals across five predeclared temperatures. At a score difference of 2 and temperature 2, expected acceptance is about 36.79%; observed acceptance was 36.988%. Every case fell within the predeclared tolerance of about 0.635 percentage points.

That tolerance uses a Hoeffding bound under ideal independent random draws. Our fixed pseudorandom streams make this a reproducible regression check, not a certification of randomness. The statistical review records all cases and assumptions. The expanded suite has 23 tests; production optimizer code and benchmark results are unchanged.

The optimizer proposes. The testing harness disposes.

A real service adds a complication: measurements fluctuate.

A noisy score can make a regression look like an improvement. Searching thousands of configurations also creates thousands of opportunities to get lucky. The most impressive single measurement may be the least trustworthy result.

For service tuning, make the evaluator earn its authority:

  1. Fix the workload, objective, constraints, and search budget before comparing methods.
  2. Repeat measurements, control warmup and machine conditions, and interleave candidates when drift could bias the comparison. Charge those repetitions to the evaluation budget.
  3. Evaluate finalists on reserved workloads, including skewed inputs, contention, and failure cases. Report variability alongside the central estimate.
  4. Check correctness and operational limits before promoting a candidate. Keep a rollback path and monitor the deployed result.

Once reserved workloads influence another round of tuning, they become development data. A fresh evaluation set is needed for a fresh generalization claim.

Accepting a worse candidate is a search decision inside an evaluation environment. It does not require deploying that candidate to customers.

Where this becomes an engineering habit

The same framing gives several everyday tuning problems a concrete shape:

Problem Candidate decisions Objective and constraints
Service performance Workers, batching, queue depth Minimize cost per completed request while meeting latency and correctness limits
AI agent orchestration Model routing, retry budget, verification threshold Minimize cost on a fixed task set while meeting quality and latency requirements
Test scheduling Test order and assignment to workers Minimize completion time while preserving the required suite and dependencies
Infrastructure sizing Instance mix, capacity, scaling thresholds Minimize cost under representative demand while meeting capacity and recovery requirements

Applying search to these problems requires a candidate representation, legal moves, and a trustworthy evaluator. In an agent system, for example, a cheap answer is useful only if the quality check deserves trust. Evaluators can be fooled or overfit too.

The separation is useful: a search proposes configurations, an evaluator measures outcomes, and a deployment process decides what can ship.

You do not need to adopt annealing to adopt that architecture.

Make annealing earn its place

Start with a baseline you can understand. If the space is small, enumerate it. If a coarse grid or random search gives good results within the budget, that is valuable evidence.

Annealing becomes interesting when useful local moves exist but a search that accepts only improvements gets trapped. Its neighborhood and temperature schedule still need attention. If objective evaluations are expensive, compare methods designed to spend fewer evaluations. If useful gradients exist, consider methods that exploit them.

The cost of tuning the optimizer also belongs in the accounting. Trying twenty cooling schedules and reporting only the best is another search, with another budget.

The engineering habit is simple: define success, constrain the experiment, compare alternatives, and keep the evidence. Repeat when the environment changes.

Sometimes a better answer is on the other side of a hill. Sometimes a simpler search already finds it. Measure which situation you are in.

What configuration have you spent hours tuning manually, and what would a trustworthy objective function for it look like?

Disclosure: AI agents drafted and revised this article, implemented the experiment, and performed technical review. The numerical results come from executing the accompanying code.

articles.title: What I Actually Learn When I Build With AI
articles.description: I've spent entire nights building something with AI, gotten a bunch of features working, and then...
articles.body_html:
I've spent entire nights building something with AI, gotten a bunch of features working, and then realized I couldn't really explain half of what I'd just built.

And then there are nights when I spend hours trying to figure out one stupid little problem, and somehow end up learning more from that than I did from the entire night before.

It's kind of funny when you think about it. Both times I was productive. Both times I ended up with working code. But what I actually learned from each experience was completely different.

I wrote a post recently about how AI is making it way too easy to avoid thinking, and it got me thinking about my own habits. Because I use AI coding tools constantly. I love them. They've helped me build things I probably wouldn't have even attempted otherwise.

But I'm also still learning. A lot.

And there is a big difference between just getting something working and actually understanding how it works.

Just because I understand the explanation doesn't mean I understand the code

This probably happens to all of us more than we'd like to admit.

I might ask AI to explain something, and it'll give me a perfectly reasonable breakdown. Everything makes sense. I can follow along, I understand what each part is doing, and I think, okay, got it.

Then 3 days later I need to change something, and suddenly I'm staring at the code like I've never seen it before.

Apparently, I understood it just fine when someone was holding my hand through the entire explanation.

That is not quite the same thing as actually knowing it, though.

And I'm not talking about memorizing syntax or remembering every little API detail. I look things up all the time, and I don't see anything wrong with that.

I'm talking about understanding why something was done a certain way.

If all I can remember about a feature is that AI wrote it and it worked, I haven't really learned much from it.

Sometimes the interesting part is the problem you didn't know existed

I've been working on a text editor called Slate, which has been a really interesting learning experience for me.

One thing I hadn't given much thought to before was what actually happens when you save a file while you're still editing it.

I mean, saving a file sounds pretty simple, right? Write the contents to disk, mark it as saved, done.

Except what happens if the user keeps typing while that save is happening?

The file being written contains the older content, but the editor now has newer changes. So if the save finishes and the editor clears the unsaved indicator, it's basically telling the user everything is saved when it isn't.

Slate uses revision-based save tracking to handle this. When a save starts, it remembers which revision of the document it's saving. That way, any changes made while the save is happening don't accidentally get marked as saved too.

Now, AI could have just implemented all of that for me. I could have tested the save button, seen that it worked, and moved on with my life.

But understanding why that revision tracking matters is what makes it useful to me.

It's not really about the code itself. It's about recognizing that something can change between the time an operation starts and the time it finishes.

And that's a problem that could come up in all kinds of applications, not just text editors.

That's the kind of thing I want to take away from a project.

Actually experimenting makes a huge difference

I've noticed the same thing when working with local AI models.

Let's say I run a model and it takes 30 seconds to complete something.

Okay, so it's slow. Right?

Well, maybe. But what actually took 30 seconds?

Was most of that time spent loading the model into memory? Was the actual processing slow? Would running it a second time be significantly faster?

Those are all things I can test.

And I find that I learn a lot more when I actually start experimenting instead of just asking AI to explain what's happening.

Run it again. Measure things separately. Change something. See what happens.

Sometimes the results are exactly what I expected. Other times they're not even close, which is usually when things get interesting.

I love that I can use AI to help me figure things out. I can ask what else I should try, or why the result isn't what I expected.

That makes learning unfamiliar things so much easier.

But there's a big difference between AI telling me why something should happen and me actually seeing what does happen.

And sometimes AI's explanation is wrong, too. Which I am sure we all know.

I don't necessarily remember the code, but I remember the problem

I think this is probably the biggest thing I've noticed.

When I really spend time understanding something, I might not remember the exact implementation later. But I remember the problem I was trying to solve and why I solved it that way.

And that carries over into other projects.

Maybe I start wondering whether some asynchronous operation could finish after the user has already changed something.

Or whether a performance issue is actually a startup issue.

Or whether I'm storing some piece of state that I could just calculate from something else.

I might still need to look things up. I might still ask AI to help me write the implementation.

But at least I know what I'm looking for and why it matters.

If I just accept the generated code without thinking much about it, I miss all of that. The solution is sitting right there in my project, but I might not even recognize the same problem when I run into it somewhere else.

And considering how often I start new projects, there's a pretty good chance I will run into it somewhere else. Probably next week.

Of course, I don't need to turn everything into a learning experience

I also think there's a balance here.

Sometimes I just want AI to fix the padding on a button.

I don't need to spend 45 minutes investigating the underlying principles of CSS spacing. I just want the button to look right.

And there are plenty of things I'm perfectly happy to let AI handle. Boilerplate, repetitive changes, things I've already done a hundred times, or just tedious work I don't feel like doing.

That's part of why I use these tools in the first place.

But when I'm building something unfamiliar, or working on functionality that I know I'll need to maintain later, I try to be a little more involved.

Sometimes that means just asking questions.

Other times I might just start changing things to see what happens.

I think even something as simple as predicting what a change will do before running it can make a difference. Because if the result isn't what I expected, now I have something to investigate.

Do I do this every time? Absolutely not.

Sometimes I've been staring at something for two hours, AI finally gets it working, and my entire thought process is basically "thank you, finally, moving on."

I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

But I am trying to be more conscious of when I'm actually learning something and when I'm just getting something done.

Because those aren't always the same thing.

Getting something working isn't the same as learning how it works

One of my favorite things about AI coding tools is how much more willing I am to try things I know very little about.

I've experimented with languages, frameworks, local models, desktop applications, and all kinds of other things that I probably would have put off before.

Not necessarily because I couldn't learn them, but because getting started on something completely unfamiliar can be a lot of work.

AI makes that initial hurdle so much smaller, and I think that's genuinely awesome.

But there's also a temptation to just keep building. One feature works, so you move on to the next one. Then the next. Before you know it, you've got a whole application and only a vague understanding of some pretty important parts of it.

And it's so easy to confuse all that progress with learning.

I've definitely done it.

I think the things that stick with me the most are usually the things I had to investigate a little. Something didn't behave the way I expected, or I got curious about why it worked a certain way, and I spent some time figuring it out.

Sometimes that investigation only takes a few minutes. Sometimes it sends me down a rabbit hole for the rest of the night.

Either way, I tend to remember those experiences a lot more than the features that worked perfectly on the first try.

And that's something I want to keep in mind as I continue building with AI.

I don't want to stop using these tools or intentionally make everything harder for myself.

I just don't want to get so caught up in how much I can build that I forget to pay attention to what I'm learning along the way.

So... what about you? Have you learned something useful while building with AI that you can now troubleshoot or explain yourself? Or have you ever gone back to AI-generated code and realized you had absolutely no idea how it worked?

articles.title: Ten findings, ten answers — publishing the audit of our own black box
articles.description: An external line-by-line audit of our flight recorder found 10 vulnerabilities. We published all ten with their file, line and severity — and answered every one in release 0.21.0, each fix carrying its own named test. 392 tests collected.
articles.body_html:
Ten findings, ten answers. That is the entire release note of NoireBox 0.21.0 — and it is the part of this month I am simultaneously proudest of and least comfortable with.

The context: NoireBox is a flight recorder for AI agents — every decision an agent takes is sealed into a hash-chained, externally anchored, tamper-evident journal. A product whose entire pitch is "you can trust what this records" has an obligation the pitch implies and can easily forget: it must survive its own audit. A recorder that audits everyone's agents but hides its own vulnerabilities is the witness-was-the-suspect problem applied to ourselves.

So we commissioned an external audit: line-by-line inspection of the v0.20.0 archive. It came back with ten findings — three high, five medium, two low — each with its file, its line numbers, and its attack path. Every finding is now public, in the audit commit, in the release notes, and in this post. Including the ones that sting.

The measured audit

The severity distribution, exactly as reported — no crypto was broken (the Ed25519 core held), but the logic around it bled:

Finding Severity One line
NB-01 high JWT secret desync: a malformed env var silently fell back to the public demo credentials demo:demo-secret
NB-02 high the third-party verifier fail-opens: missing openssl or ots on the machine → return True
NB-03 high custody-drift bypass via a forged anchor event, and a terminal-records overwrite that could swallow a proven race
NB-04 medium SSRF: an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address walked past the link-local check
NB-05 medium Merkle tree collisions: odd-leaf duplication and no RFC 6962 domain separation
NB-06 medium DoS: unbounded EventIn payloads plus store.all() re-verifying the whole journal per public GET
NB-07 medium no rate limiting on the token endpoint, and an unbounded rate-limiter memory
NB-08 medium joblib.load() deserialization without a prior SHA-256 check
NB-09 low the container ran as root, listening on 0.0.0.0
NB-10 low tool inputs sealed into the immutable journal unredacted — secrets included

Ten findings across auth, verification, networking, cryptography-adjacent logic, resource handling, and secrets handling. None broke the cryptography. All of them were real. The report cites file and line for each — the auditor's receipts, not adjectives.

Three findings, three answers

NB-02 is the one that should frighten every builder of verification tooling. The third-party verifier fail-opens: if openssl or the ots tool is missing on the machine, the check returns True with the string "reported, not hidden." Any CI/CD pipeline validating a journal inside a distroless container — no openssl, no ots — would validate a journal whose timestamp tokens were completely forged, "tsr": "AAAA". The verifier that reports "not verified" as a pass is the most dangerous line in the file: it converts an absence of tooling into a presence of trust.

The answer in 0.21.0: unverifiable witness tokens exit 2, never the clean 0. The project's doctrine — undecidable is never clean — now applies to the tool that enforces it too. Legacy pipelines that need the old behavior pay for it explicitly: --allow-unverified-witnesses or NOIREBOX_ALLOW_UNVERIFIED_WITNESSES=1. The escape hatch survives; it is priced.

NB-03 is the one that proves the premises table works. The audit found that a forged anchor event — {"head_seq": 999999, "head_hash": "faux"}, no timestamp authority — would pass the custody grader unnoticed, and that a non-terminal record could overwrite a proven verdict_predates_terminal race, making the finding vanish. Both closed in 0.21.0: the anchor input now validates the cited head hash and token presence, and the non-terminal overwrite surfaces as post_terminal_activity. Each fix carries its own named test.

NB-01 is the one every demo-mode product should read. The JWT secret desynced from the loaded key, and a malformed NOIREBOX_CLIENTS env var silently fell back to the public demo credentials — the operator believed authentication was on; the app had switched to demo:demo-secret. The answer: the app now refuses to start rather than guess, and the secret derives from the key actually loaded. Fail loudly at startup beats fail quietly at request time.

The full mapping — all ten findings, all ten answers, version by version — is in the release notes. Every fix carries its own named test: 392 collected at release time.

The species-blind argument, again — with better data

Last week's audit arc (an external reader descending our reconciliation layer) proved the method on a sample of one probe. This audit is the second data point, from a different species of reviewer: a line-by-line inspection agent rather than a human prober. Two external entities, two methods, same conclusion: external entities find what internal reviews confess and defer. The internal review had labeled NB-02's weakness in writing; it took the external pass to make its closure a release blocker. McGraw's advice — "get an external entity to help" — is not consulting wisdom. It is the mechanism by which the ladder grew its floor.

The code, verbatim

Four excerpts from v0.20.0, unchanged. First, the verifier that reports "not verified" as a pass — two functions, same shape:

# verifier/verifier.py
def verify_anchor_token(...):
    if not shutil.which("openssl"):
        return True, "openssl missing — token not verified (reported, not hidden)", False

def verify_ots_token(...):
    ...
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
        return True, "ots verify timed out (reported, not hidden)", False

Second, the register a race can zero — the custody grader trusted whatever anchor arrived last, without checking that its hash matched the real event:

# noirebox/reconcile.py
def _newest_anchor(events: list[dict]) -> dict | None:
    newest = None
    for e in events:
        if e.get("type") == "anchor":
            seq = e.get("payload", {}).get("head_seq")
            if seq is not None and (newest is None or seq > newest["head_seq"]):
                newest = {"head_seq": int(seq), ...}

Third, the premise under the JWT: the secret reloaded from a hardcoded path on every request, ignoring the key the app had already loaded — plus the fallback clients dict:

# noirebox/auth.py
DEFAULT_CLIENTS = {"demo": "demo-secret"}

def _jwt_secret():
    ...
    key = KeyPair.load_or_create(
        os.environ.get("NOIREBOX_DB", "data/noirebox.db") + ".key")

And the deserialization with no integrity gate:

# noirebox/ml_guardrail.py
_pipelines[lang] = joblib.load(path)

Read them in that order and the severity calls grade themselves: two fail-opens that answer "trust me", one race with no validation, one hardcoded path, one pickle. None subtle. All shipped for months — which is the part the next audit is for.

What to steal — the pattern, generalized

  • Commission an external line-by-line audit of your own tool, on the current version, before someone else does it for you.
  • Publish the findings with file, line, and severity — the auditor's receipts, not your summary of them.
  • Answer every finding in one release, each answer carrying its own named test — "ten findings, ten answers" is a sentence a user can verify in an evening.
  • Keep the premises table public. The findings your answers did not close, the assumptions your controls rest on, the hardening deliberately deferred — labeled, public, falsifiable.

Two honest limits

The auditor was an agent we commissioned, on a version we chose. An n=1 external probe with a scope we set is not the same as a red team with its own budget and its own grudge. And every finding was logic-level — the Ed25519 core held, no cryptographic break — which is both genuinely good and partially luck of scope.

And "ten answers" is young. Release 0.21.0 is days old; 392 tests collected is a snapshot, not a track record. The real test of "ten findings, ten answers" is the next audit — whether the new premises table holds, and whether the answers aged into defenses or into new residues. That audit is already scheduled. Its findings will be published too — that sentence is the commitment, and now it is on the record.

Your turn

The audit findings are public, the answers are in the repo, and the premises table names what still stands. If you ship anything agents touch — audit it externally, publish the findings with your answers, and link both. The registry of published self-audits in this lane is empty. Being first costs one uncomfortable week. Being second costs the excuse.
