articles.title: What a Hexagonal Port Costs in Go: itabs, Escape Analysis and a Postgres Round Trip
articles.description: A Go port costs an itab load and an indirect call. The real price is escape analysis. A runnable benchmark, then a Postgres round trip for scale.
articles.body_html:
• Book: Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

You put a UserRepository interface between your domain and Postgres. The review comes back with one line: "Interfaces are slow in Go. Just pass the pool."

That objection is half right, and the half that is right is not the one people argue about. The dispatch itself is a pointer load and an indirect call. What costs you is that the compiler cannot see through the interface, so it stops inlining and starts sending values to the heap. That second part is a known, open compiler limitation: golang/go#36964 has tracked it since February 2020.

You can check all of this yourself with one benchmark file and -gcflags=-m.

What your domain holds: two words and an itab

An interface with methods is two machine words. The current layout lives in internal/abi/iface.go:

type NonEmptyInterface struct {
    ITab *ITab
    Data unsafe.Pointer
}

type ITab struct {
    Inter *InterfaceType
    Type  *Type
    Hash  uint32     // copy of Type.Hash
    Fun   [1]uintptr // variable sized
}

Data points at your adapter, say a *pgRepo. ITab points at a table pairing the interface type with the concrete type, followed by one function pointer per method. The source comment says itabs are allocated in non-garbage-collected memory, and runtime/iface.go keeps them in a global table it reads without locks on the common path. They are built once, not per call.

The call repo.Save(ctx, u) then does what Russ Cox described back in Go Data Structures: Interfaces (2009): the equivalent of tab->fun[0](data). Load the itab pointer, load the function pointer, call it with the data word as the receiver.


An interface value is two words: an itab pointer and a data pointer.

Vicent Martí spelled out what that indirection costs in PlanetScale's 2022 generics deep dive: a call through an interface prevents inlining. Lose inlining and you also lose the optimizations it would have opened up. (Devirtualization, below, is the exception.)

Where it costs you: escape analysis gives up at the interface

Escape analysis decides whether a value can live on the stack. To decide, it has to see every function the pointer is handed to. Through an interface, it can't: the callee is whatever sits in the itab at runtime.

In #36964, a Go compiler contributor explains the bind: at the moment you allocate the value, the compiler may not know which interface methods it will be passed to. So it assumes the worst. A pointer argument to an interface method escapes, even when every implementation you ship only reads it.

The receiver side has its own open issue. #62653, "avoid always escaping the receivers in interface method calls", is milestoned for Go 1.28 after moving from 1.27 in June 2026. A March 2026 report, #78336, shows a non-pointer value stored in an interface being heap-allocated through runtime.convT64 because a method is called on it.

That is the second allocation source to know about. Since Go 1.4, interface values always hold a pointer, so storing a non-pointer value in an interface means boxing it. The runtime skips the allocation for integers under 256 (staticuint64s) and for empty strings, and allocates otherwise. A logging decorator that passes u.ID into a ...any argument pays that on every call once your IDs pass 255.

A benchmark you can run: direct, port, decorated port

Run go mod init portcost in an empty directory and save what follows as port_test.go. One file, no dependencies. The first part is the domain type, the port, an in-memory adapter and a decorator:

package portcost

import (
    "context"
    "sync/atomic"
    "testing"
)

type User struct {
    ID    int64
    Name  string
    Email string
}

type UserRepository interface {
    Save(ctx context.Context, u *User) error
}

type memRepo struct{ last int64 }

func (r *memRepo) Save(ctx context.Context, u *User) error {
    r.last = u.ID
    return nil
}

// A decorator, the way metrics or logging wraps a port.
type counting struct {
    next  UserRepository
    calls atomic.Int64
}

func (r *counting) Save(ctx context.Context, u *User) error {
    r.calls.Add(1)
    return r.next.Save(ctx, u)
}

Below it, in the same file, go two services that are identical except for the field type, and a benchmark for each setup. The //go:noinline on both Rename methods is deliberate: it keeps the outer call identical, so the only difference is what happens inside.

type Direct struct{ repo *memRepo }

//go:noinline
func (s *Direct) Rename(ctx context.Context, id int64) error {
    u := User{ID: id, Name: "renamed"}
    return s.repo.Save(ctx, &u)
}

type Ported struct{ repo UserRepository }

//go:noinline
func (s *Ported) Rename(ctx context.Context, id int64) error {
    u := User{ID: id, Name: "renamed"}
    return s.repo.Save(ctx, &u)
}

var bg = context.Background()

func BenchmarkDirect(b *testing.B) {
    s := &Direct{repo: &memRepo{}}
    for b.Loop() {
        _ = s.Rename(bg, 42)
    }
}

func BenchmarkPort(b *testing.B) {
    s := &Ported{repo: &memRepo{}}
    for b.Loop() {
        _ = s.Rename(bg, 42)
    }
}

func BenchmarkPortDecorated(b *testing.B) {
    s := &Ported{repo: &counting{next: &memRepo{}}}
    for b.Loop() {
        _ = s.Rename(bg, 42)
    }
}

b.Loop needs Go 1.24 or newer. Before Go 1.26 it also blocked inlining in the loop body, which is one more reason for the //go:noinline pins: the outer call stays the same on every version. Run the benchmarks with allocation counts, and ask the compiler what it decided:

go test -bench . -benchmem -count 5
go test -run '^$' -bench . -gcflags=-m 2>&1 \
  | grep -E 'heap|devirt|inlin'

I haven't run this myself, so there are no numbers here; yours are the ones that count anyway. In the -m output, Direct.Rename should show inlining call to (*memRepo).Save and no heap line for u. Ported.Rename is where you'd expect moved to heap: u, because &u goes into an interface method the compiler can't see. Those message formats come straight from the compiler's inliner, escape and devirtualize passes.

In the benchmark output, compare the allocs/op column before you look at ns/op. The decorated version adds a second indirect call plus an atomic add, which is about what a metrics decorator costs in production.

If -m prints nothing, the build came from cache. Touch the file and run it again.

When the compiler deletes the port for you

The devirtualize package runs two passes. The static one rewrites an interface call into a direct call when the concrete type is known at compile time, and -m reports it as devirtualizing ... to .... This is the classic benchmark trap: write var r UserRepository = &memRepo{} and call r.Save in the same function, and you are timing a direct call while thinking you're timing a port. If a devirtualizing line points at the line inside Ported.Rename, your port benchmark isn't measuring a port.

The second pass is profile-guided. Go 1.21 made PGO ready for general use and added devirtualization of interface calls to the most common callee. Go 1.22 widened it and interleaved devirtualization with inlining. The rewrite is a guarded direct call with the original call as fallback, shaped like this in the compiler's own doc comment:

if c, ok := i.(Concrete); ok {
    c.Foo()
} else {
    i.Foo()
}

Two details from the source matter for ports. The pass skips callees it knows won't inline, because inlining is the whole point. And -pgo=auto only picks up default.pgo for main packages, per the go command docs, so in a test you pass the profile yourself:

go test -run '^$' -bench PortDecorated -cpuprofile cpu.pprof
go test -run '^$' -bench . -benchmem -pgo=cpu.pprof \
  -gcflags=-m 2>&1 | grep -i 'pgo devirtualizing'

Notice that the fallback branch is still an ordinary interface call. My reading is that &u still flows into an unknown method there, so check whether moved to heap: u survives in the PGO build before you count on the allocation going away. For whole programs, the PGO guide reports 2 to 14% runtime gains across a representative set of Go programs as of Go 1.22.

Put it next to one Postgres round trip

Add a second file, pg_test.go, in the same directory. It uses pgx through database/sql (run go get github.com/jackc/pgx/v5 first) and skips itself unless you point it at a database.

package portcost

import (
    "database/sql"
    "os"
    "testing"

    _ "github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/stdlib"
)

func BenchmarkPostgresRoundTrip(b *testing.B) {
    dsn := os.Getenv("PG_DSN")
    if dsn == "" {
        b.Skip("set PG_DSN to run")
    }
    db, err := sql.Open("pgx", dsn)
    if err != nil {
        b.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer db.Close()
    if err := db.PingContext(bg); err != nil {
        b.Fatal(err)
    }
    var one int
    for b.Loop() {
        row := db.QueryRowContext(bg, "SELECT 1")
        if err := row.Scan(&one); err != nil {
            b.Fatal(err)
        }
    }
}

Run it against the database your service actually talks to, not a laptop container, and divide. For a rough anchor before you have your own numbers, the latency table attributed to Jeff Dean puts a round trip within one datacenter at 500,000 ns and a branch mispredict at 5 ns. The table is old and your network is not Google's, but the ratio is the point: even if every port call cost as much as a mispredicted branch, one query would pay for about 100,000 of them, before the server does any work.


Dispatch and one database round trip are not on the same scale.

The allocation is the part worth watching. One small heap object per call is cheap on its own, and Go 1.27 made some allocations under 80 bytes up to 30% cheaper. It adds up when a port sits inside a loop that runs per row or per item: a PriceRule interface called 100,000 times per request is a design problem. A UserRepository called twice per request, each time followed by a network trip, is not.

So keep ports where hexagonal architecture puts them anyway, at the I/O boundary. Pass batches across them, not single items in a tight loop. And when a reviewer says interfaces are slow, send them the -benchmem output and the SELECT 1 number side by side.

If this was useful

The benchmark tells you what a port costs. Where it belongs is the question Hexagonal Architecture in Go is built around: which interfaces the domain owns, how persistence adapters plug in, and how to lay out the packages so the boundary stays at the I/O edge. If you want the architecture side of what you just measured, start with the book here. It's half of the Thinking in Go series.

articles.title: Why collapsible tab headers jump in React Native (and how to fix it)
articles.description: You've seen this screen a hundred times: a profile header, a row of tabs underneath (Posts, Media,...
articles.body_html:
You've seen this screen a hundred times: a profile header, a row of tabs underneath (Posts, Media, Likes), and the header collapses as you scroll. Twitter, Instagram, Spotify artist pages.

Now try this on most implementations:

  1. Scroll Posts down a few screens. The header collapses.
  2. Switch to Media, which is still at the top.
  3. Watch the header jump: snap open, snap closed, or leave a gap.

I hit this enough times that I ended up writing my own library. Here's what's actually going on.

The root cause: the header is derived from the active tab's scroll

The common approach is simple: headerTranslateY = -clamp(activeTab.scrollY, 0, headerHeight).

It works perfectly with one tab. With several, every tab has its own scroll offset, and the header position is a function of whichever tab is active. Switch tabs and the input changes instantly, so the output (your header) teleports.

Libraries usually patch around it by force-syncing scroll offsets on every tab switch (scrolling the new tab to match the header). That's where you get flicker, lost scroll positions, and fights with list virtualization.

The fix: decouple the header from tab offsets

Instead of deriving the header from a scroll offset, make the header position its own piece of state (a Reanimated shared value), and drive it with scroll deltas:

  • Scrolling down collapses the header in sync with content.
  • Scrolling up keeps the header collapsed until the content's top edge reaches it, then expands it in sync. The header never detaches from content and never leaves a gap.
  • Switching tabs doesn't touch the header at all. Each tab keeps its own scroll position, and the header stays exactly where it was.

No offset-syncing, no jump, and every tab remembers where you left it.

The trade-off (there's always one)

Because each tab keeps its own scroll memory, a deep-scrolled tab can have content sitting underneath an expanded header. So the header needs a solid background; translucent headers don't work with this model. I think that's the right trade for jump-free switching, but it's worth knowing upfront.

In practice

▶️ Watch the demo: switching tabs with zero header jump

I packaged this approach as react-native-collapsible-tab. It's built on Reanimated, Gesture Handler and Pager View, with all animation on the UI thread.

npm install react-native-collapsible-tab
npx expo install react-native-reanimated react-native-gesture-handler react-native-pager-view

import { Tabs } from 'react-native-collapsible-tab';

function Profile() {
  return (
    <Tabs.Container
      renderHeader={() => <ProfileHeader />} // height measured automatically
      minHeaderHeight={insets.top}           // stays visible when collapsed
      lazy                                   // mount tabs on first focus
      snapThreshold={0.5}                    // settle fully open/closed on release
    >
      <Tabs.Tab name="posts" label="Posts">
        <Tabs.FlatList
          data={posts}
          renderItem={({ item }) => <Post post={item} />}
          keyExtractor={(item) => item.id}
        />
      </Tabs.Tab>
      <Tabs.Tab name="media" label="Media">
        <Tabs.ScrollView>
          <MediaGrid />
        </Tabs.ScrollView>
      </Tabs.Tab>
    </Tabs.Container>
  );
}

A few things I cared about while building it:

  • Twitter-style reveal: revealHeaderOnScroll brings the header back on any upward scroll.
  • Snap without deadlocks: snap is a plain shared-value animation, not offset-driven scrolling, which is known to lock up the UI thread on the New Architecture.
  • FlashList v2 and LegendList adapters, plus FlatList, ScrollView and SectionList.
  • Windowed memory: with React 19.2's <Activity>, windowConfig={{ ahead: 1, behind: 1 }} keeps 60 tabs from all staying mounted. Only the focused one and its neighbours stay live, and scroll positions survive.

One gotcha that bites everyone: negative scroll offsets

If you animate anything from scroll position (a progress bar, a fade), remember that on iOS contentOffset.y goes negative when the list bounces past the top. Android clamps at 0. Clamp both ends:

// ❌ negative offset → negative width during bounce
width: `${Math.min((scrollY.value / TOTAL) * 100, 100)}%`

// ✅ overscroll reads as 0%
width: `${Math.max(0, Math.min((scrollY.value / TOTAL) * 100, 100))}%`

bounces={false} hides the symptom; clamping is the actual fix.

Docs: rnct.scannertechs.com · GitHub: JassiSingh08/react-native-collapsible-tab

If you've fought this bug with a different approach, I'd love to hear how you solved it in the comments.

articles.title: Stripping EXIF and GPS from photos in the browser, losslessly, in ~500 lines of vanilla JS
articles.description: Photos from phones carry more than pixels. Open the file and there's often the exact GPS position it...
articles.body_html:
Photos from phones carry more than pixels. Open the file and there's often the exact GPS position it was taken at, the phone model, lens and settings, the date and time, sometimes the owner's name or a camera serial number, and, increasingly, labels saying whether an image was edited with generative AI.

I make a small Android camera app, and people kept asking whether the photos they share give away where they live. So I built a checker that shows what a photo file carries and saves a clean copy, without uploading anything:

https://blinqdroid.com/tools/photo-privacy-check/

No libraries, no server, no WebAssembly: a DataView over the file's bytes. Here's how it works.

Reading the file without uploading it

The whole thing starts with the bytes in memory:

const u8 = new Uint8Array(await file.arrayBuffer());

From there it's container walking. The first bytes tell you the format: FF D8 is a JPEG, 89 PNG is a PNG, RIFF....WEBP is a WebP, and II/MM at the start is a TIFF (which is also what a DNG raw file is).

JPEG: walking the markers

A JPEG is a list of segments. Each starts with 0xFF, a marker byte, then a two-byte big-endian length:

let p = 2; // skip SOI (FF D8)
while (p + 4 <= u8.length) {
  if (u8[p] !== 0xFF) { p++; continue; }
  const m = u8[p + 1];
  const len = (u8[p + 2] << 8) | u8[p + 3];
  const start = p + 4, n = len - 2;
  if (m === 0xE1 && ascii(u8, start, 6) === 'Exif\0\0') readTiff(u8, start + 6, n - 6);
  // APP1 can also hold XMP: "http://ns.adobe.com/xap/1.0/\0" + XML
  p = start + n;
}

The fiddly part is the image data itself. After a Start of Scan (FF DA) segment comes entropy-coded data with no length field. Inside it, a literal 0xFF byte is "stuffed" as FF 00, and restart markers FF D0–FF D7 can appear. So to find the next real segment (progressive JPEGs have several scans, with tables in between) you scan forward for an 0xFF that is followed by something other than 00 or a restart marker.

EXIF is a tiny TIFF file

The EXIF block is a TIFF structure: a byte-order mark (II little-endian, MM big-endian), the number 42, and an offset to the first IFD (image file directory). Each IFD entry is 12 bytes: tag, type, count, and either the value or an offset to it.

const le = ascii(u8, base, 2) === 'II';
const dv = new DataView(u8.buffer, u8.byteOffset + base);
const count = dv.getUint16(ifdOffset, le);
for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
  const e = ifdOffset + 2 + i * 12;
  const tag = dv.getUint16(e, le), type = dv.getUint16(e + 2, le);
  // 0x8769 points to the Exif sub-IFD, 0x8825 to the GPS IFD
}

GPS coordinates are three rationals (degrees, minutes, seconds), each a pair of 32-bit integers, plus a reference letter:

const dms = ([d, m, s], ref) => (d + m / 60 + s / 3600) * (/[SW]/.test(ref) ? -1 : 1);

The IFD after the first one (IFD1) is the embedded thumbnail. It's easy to forget, and it can still show the uncropped original after you've cropped the photo.

PNG, WebP and the AI labels

PNG is a list of chunks (length, type, data, CRC). Metadata lives in eXIf (the same TIFF structure), tEXt/iTXt/zTXt text chunks and tIME. Some image generators write their whole prompt into a tEXt chunk called parameters, so the tool shows text chunks verbatim.

WebP is RIFF: four-character chunk IDs with little-endian sizes, padded to even lengths. EXIF and XMP are separate chunks, and the VP8X header has flag bits saying they're present.

In XMP, the interesting fields for 2026 are the IPTC DigitalSourceType values (trainedAlgorithmicMedia means made with generative AI, compositeWithTrainedAlgorithmicMedia edited with it) and whether a Content Credentials (C2PA) manifest is embedded. The tool only detects C2PA; it doesn't validate the signature.

Cleaning without re-compressing

The easy way to strip metadata is to draw the image on a canvas and export it. That re-encodes the JPEG and loses quality. Instead, for JPEG, PNG and WebP the tool rebuilds the file from the parts it keeps:

  • JPEG: keep everything except APP1–APP15 and COM segments, with two exceptions: the ICC colour profile (APP2 "ICC_PROFILE") and Adobe's APP14, because dropping those changes how colours display. The image data is copied byte for byte.
  • PNG: drop eXIf, tEXt, iTXt, zTXt, tIME and the C2PA caBX chunk.
  • WebP: drop EXIF and XMP chunks, clear their bits in VP8X, and rewrite the RIFF size.

One catch with JPEGs: phones often store the image sideways and add an Orientation tag saying how to display it. Strip all EXIF and the photo shows up rotated. So the clean JPEG gets a brand-new 36-byte EXIF segment containing exactly one tag, Orientation, and nothing else.

Other formats the browser can decode (AVIF, for example) fall back to a canvas re-encode as JPEG at quality 0.95. DNG is read-only, and HEIC can only be cleaned in browsers that can decode it.

Proving it worked

Before offering the download, the page runs the same parser on the clean copy and reports anything left. It's a small step, but it turns "trust me" into "here's what the output contains":

const again = summary(analyse(new Uint8Array(await blob.arrayBuffer())));
const left = ['location', 'identity', 'device', 'time', 'software', 'ai'].filter(k => again[k].length);

Privacy, verifiably

The page runs under a strict Content Security Policy (no inline scripts, no third-party scripts), and the photo never leaves the tab: load the page, switch off your network, and it still works. The script isn't minified, so you can read it at /js/photo-check.js. The only request it makes is to my own page counter, saying that a photo was checked or cleaned. There are no cookies and no photo data in it.

If you find a file it misreads, I'd love to hear about it in the comments: the metadata, not the photo, or a test file with fake details.

articles.title: When Does Claude Code Check the Web? I Logged My Sessions to Find Out
articles.description: On October 12, 2026, AWS launched Lambda Web Functions. You can now run a normal Express or Next.js...
articles.body_html:
On October 12, 2026, AWS launched Lambda Web Functions. You can now run a normal Express or Next.js app on Lambda, with up to 128 concurrent requests per execution environment.

Two days later I asked three Claude models in Claude Code: "Our Express app is in app.js. Add the files needed to deploy it to AWS Lambda with the fewest moving parts."

All six runs wrote a setup that was the best answer until October 11: serverless-http, serverless-express, or the Lambda Web Adapter. Five of them looked nothing up. The sixth only checked the latest version of serverless-http on npm.

Then I asked "What's the newest way to run an Express app on AWS Lambda, as of this month?" Every run searched the web. Five of six named Web Functions.

The topic was the same. Only the wording changed. I wanted to know how far that goes. When does Claude Code look things up, and when does it answer from its training data? And when it answers from training data, how often is the answer out of date?

The setup

Seven topics that changed after the models' training cutoff (June 2026). I checked each one against the official source on the day of the test:

Topic Current fact Since
Lambda Web Functions new Lambda form factor for HTTP apps 2026-10-12
Lambda Python runtimes python3.14 GA, python3.15 in preview 2025-11 / 2026-08
actions/setup-node v7 2026-07-14
openai Python SDK 3.x, built on HTTPX2, no longer installs httpx 2026-08-12
Stripe API version 2026-09-30.endive 2026-09-30
Django 6.1 2026-08-05
Python 3.15.0 2026-10-09

Three ways to ask about each topic:

  • Neutral question: "Which major version of actions/setup-node should a GitHub workflow use?"
  • Time cue: "What's the latest major version of actions/setup-node today?"
  • Coding task: "Add a GitHub Actions workflow that runs npm test on every push."

Plus three stable controls, like "What does HTTP status 409 mean?"

That makes 24 prompts. I ran them on Haiku 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Opus 5.5, two trials each: 144 sessions. Each one was a fresh headless session in a small repo (an Express app, a Python Lambda handler, a README):

claude -p "<prompt>" --model <model> --output-format stream-json --verbose \
  --max-turns 10 --permission-mode acceptEdits \
  --allowedTools "Read,Glob,Grep,Edit,Write,WebFetch,WebSearch,Bash,PowerShell,ToolSearch"

Before each run, the repo is reset with git and there is no project memory.

What counts as a web call: WebFetch, WebSearch, and shell commands that reach the network. That last group matters. Claude often skips WebFetch and calls gh api, curl against the PyPI JSON API, pip index versions, or git ls-remote --tags.

Grading. A Sonnet subagent graded each of the 126 non-control answers against the ground truth table, as one of three grades:

  • current: uses the current fact as a fact.
  • hedged: old or unsure, but tells the user it may be out of date.
  • stale: presents old information as current.

For coding tasks it also graded the file the model wrote. I checked the grades by hand and changed four of them (see Limits).

Finding 1: the trigger is the words, not the topic

Share of runs with at least one web call:

Stable control Neutral question Coding task Time cue
Haiku 5.5 0/6 8/14 5/14 14/14
Sonnet 5.5 0/6 7/14 4/14 14/14
Opus 5.5 0/6 12/14 7/14 14/14

"Latest", "today", "right now", "as of this month": 42 out of 42 runs looked it up. Stable questions: 0 out of 18. That part works as you would hope.

The middle columns are where it gets interesting. Within them, the pattern depends on what kind of question it is:

  • "Which version should I use?" usually triggers a lookup. For setup-node, Lambda Python runtimes, and Stripe API versions, 18 of 18 neutral runs checked.
  • "How do I use this API?" never does. "How do I pass a custom httpx client with a proxy to the OpenAI Python SDK?" got 0 lookups in 6 runs. None mentioned that version 3 exists. Five of six used httpx.Client, which fails on a fresh install of the current SDK (details below). One Opus run used the SDK's DefaultHttpxClient, which still works.
  • "Can this service do X?" depends on the model. "Can AWS Lambda serve many concurrent HTTP requests from one execution environment?" Haiku and Sonnet answered from memory every time ("no, one request per environment"). Opus searched both times. More on what it found below.

Finding 2: no lookup means a stale answer, and usually no warning

Here is every graded answer, split by whether the session made a web call:

Runs Current Hedged Stale
With a web call 85 69 (81%) 12 4
Without a web call 41 3 (7%) 7 31 (76%)

The three "current" answers without a web call were all Opus on the OpenAI topic. Each used the SDK's own DefaultHttpxClient helper, which version 3 still supports. In the two coding runs, Opus also ran the code against the installed package, which happened to be the current version. None of the three knew that version 3 exists. The code worked because the SDK kept an old name. Apart from that one case, no answer from training data alone was current.

That is expected for facts that changed after the cutoff. What I didn't expect was how rarely the models said so. Of the 35 stale answers, 28 gave no warning at all. The other 7 had some caveat, but often a narrow or generic one. For example, one answer warned about checking the Lambda Web Adapter layer version, but it didn't know Web Functions existed.

When Sonnet did hedge, the hedges were good ones: "Django 6.1 if it is out, I'm not sure it has shipped", "I answered from memory and did not check". When it hedged, it meant it.

Finding 3: coding tasks are the blind spot

Here is what ended up in the files for the coding tasks that did not mention "newest":

Task Web lookups What was written (6 runs) Current
GitHub workflow running npm test 0/6 setup-node@v4 (Haiku, Sonnet), @v5 (Opus) v7
SAM template for a Python Lambda 0/6 python3.13 (5 runs), python3.12 (1 run) python3.14
OpenAI client through a proxy 0/6 import httpx + httpx.Client(proxy=...) (Haiku, Sonnet), DefaultHttpxClient (Opus) DefaultHttpx2Client
Express app on Lambda 1/6 serverless-http, serverless-express, Lambda Web Adapter Web Functions
Stripe client with a pinned API version 3/6 2026-09-30.endive (3), 2025-09-30.clover, 2025-03-31.basil, 2024-06-20 2026-09-30.endive

The Stripe row shows it best. Opus searched in both runs and pinned the current version. Haiku searched in one of two runs and got it right in that one. Sonnet never searched and pinned versions from 2025.

Two coding tasks did trigger lookups every time: "pin Django to the newest stable version" and "a Dockerfile on the newest stable Python". 12 out of 12. The word "newest" in the coding task was enough.

The OpenAI row needs a note, because "outdated" can mean "still works". I checked it in a clean virtual environment with only openai==3.31.0 installed. The Haiku and Sonnet code fails on its first line:

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'httpx'

openai 3.x depends on httpx2 and no longer pulls in httpx. In an older environment that still has httpx, the same code runs. The Opus version uses the SDK's own DefaultHttpxClient, which 3.x keeps as an alias built on httpx2. That one works on a fresh install too.

Finding 4: the training data is older than the cutoff

These models have a June 2026 training cutoff. But look at what the coding tasks wrote:

  • Lambda added python3.14 on November 18, 2025, seven months before the cutoff. All six SAM templates used 3.13 or 3.12.
  • actions/setup-node v6 shipped in October 2025. Haiku and Sonnet wrote v4 (2023). Opus wrote v5 (September 2025).
  • Haiku pinned Stripe API version 2024-06-20.

So "the model knows things up to its cutoff" is too generous for coding defaults. My guess at the reason: when a model writes a version from memory, it writes the version it saw most in training. That is the version most existing code used, often a year or two behind the cutoff. The newest versions are thin in the training data, because little code used them yet.

The practical effect: checking whether something changed after the cutoff is not enough. A version pinned from memory can be stale even for things released well before it.

Finding 5: a lookup is not the same as a current answer

Four stale answers came after a web call. They show two different ways a search can fail.

The search asked about what the model already knew. On "Can AWS Lambda serve many concurrent HTTP requests from one execution environment?", Opus searched both times. Both times the query was:

AWS Lambda Managed Instances multi-concurrency execution environment

Lambda Managed Instances is a real feature from late 2025. Opus knew it from training, searched to confirm it, and got a good, sourced answer about Managed Instances. It never found Web Functions, launched two days earlier, which is the direct answer to the question. The search was built from the model's memory, so it could only confirm that memory.

The search index was behind. Python 3.15.0 came out on October 9. On October 14, Sonnet searched "latest stable Python release python.org downloads" and got cached snapshots of python.org listing 3.14.8 as the newest release and 3.15 as a pre-release. It wrote python:3.14-slim into the Dockerfile. In a different run, the query "latest stable Python release version October 2026" found 3.15. The search with the month in it worked. The one without it got old snapshots.

To be fair, Sonnet said it got the version from a web search. And when asked the plain question ("What is the newest stable Python release today?"), it got the same stale snapshots. Both times it said the search results disagreed, and once it added that 3.15 "may have shipped since". It was honest about the gap. In the Dockerfile run, it still wrote the old version.

Finding 6: one line in CLAUDE.md fixes most of it

If the gap is that coding tasks don't trigger lookups, the obvious fix is to tell the model to look things up. I added this CLAUDE.md to the repo and reran the seven coding tasks, 3 models x 2 trials:

Your training data may be out of date. Before you write any version number,
runtime identifier, GitHub Action version, API version, or SDK usage pattern
into a file, look up the current value (web, package registry, or official
docs). Prefer the newest stable option unless the repo pins something else.

Coding tasks with a web lookup went from 16 of 42 runs to 42 of 42. Answers graded current went from 15 of 42 to 33 of 42.

Per task, files with the current value (6 runs each):

Task Without CLAUDE.md With CLAUDE.md
GitHub workflow (setup-node) 0/6 6/6 (@v7)
SAM template (Python runtime) 0/6 6/6 (python3.14)
Stripe client (API version) 3/6 6/6 (2026-09-30.endive)
OpenAI client through a proxy 2/6 work 4/6 (DefaultHttpx2Client), Haiku still wrote import httpx
Django requirements ("newest") 6/6 6/6
Dockerfile ("newest" Python) 5/6 5/6
Express app on Lambda 0/6 0/6 (Opus found Web Functions, then ran out of turns)

Version pins are fixed. The two tasks that already said "newest" didn't change, because they were already looking things up.

Two things the rule did not fully fix:

Haiku looked up the version, not the API. On the OpenAI task, Haiku checked the latest version on PyPI both times. It then wrote the same import httpx code as before. It treated "look up" as "find the version number", not "find out how the SDK is used now". Sonnet and Opus read the SDK README and wrote DefaultHttpx2Client.

The approach changed only for the models that read past the version number. Haiku and Sonnet used the rule to look up versions for the approach they had already chosen from memory: the latest serverless-http on npm, the latest Lambda Web Adapter layer, the latest Node runtime. One Sonnet run also opened the AWS page on Web Functions runtimes. It then named Web Functions as an alternative and explained why it didn't use them: app.js would need a small change, and it wasn't sure SAM supports them yet. That's a reasonable call. The other Haiku and Sonnet runs never mentioned Web Functions.

Opus went further. In both runs, the Lambda runtimes page led it to Web Functions. It then read the Web Functions runtimes page, the samples, the "create" guide, and the aws lambda-web deploy CLI reference. It was clearly heading for the new approach. Then both runs hit my 10-turn limit before writing a file. So I can't say what it would have written, only that the rule made it find the feature that launched two days earlier.

The cost of the rule: across the 42 coding runs, the total went from $2.51 to $4.47 (+78%), and Sonnet's average time went from 10 to 18 seconds. For setup work that pins versions, that's cheap. For every small edit, you may not want it.

The models compared

Avg web calls per run Coding tasks graded current Cost for 48 runs
Haiku 5.5 1.08 4/14 $0.57
Sonnet 5.5 0.81 3/14 $2.02
Opus 5.5 1.33 8/14 $5.68

Opus looks things up the most, mostly on neutral questions (12 of 14 against 7 or 8 for the others), and it is the only one that searched on the Stripe coding task both times. Haiku searched more than Sonnet. Sonnet was the most likely to answer from memory, and also the most likely to say so.

Costs are the total_cost_usd Claude Code reports per session. The whole experiment cost about $8.30 for the 144 main runs, plus $4.50 for the 42 CLAUDE.md runs.

Limits

  • Two trials per model. The patterns were very stable across trials, but rare behavior won't show up.
  • Seven topics. All are developer tooling with a version number or a launch date. I didn't test topics where "what changed" is fuzzier.
  • Headless sessions with acceptEdits. An interactive session may behave a bit differently.
  • One grader, a Sonnet subagent, with my spot checks. I changed four grades in two cases. One rewarded a generic "AWS may have changed" footer. In the other three, old-style OpenAI code turned out to still work on the new SDK.
  • A 10-turn cap. Both Opus runs of the Express task with the CLAUDE.md rule hit it while reading the Web Functions docs, so they wrote no files. With a higher cap, that row would probably look better for Opus.
  • The test date was close to the launches on purpose. Lambda Web Functions were two days old. That is the hardest case, and the most realistic one for "what changed last week".

What I take from this

Time words are the trigger. "Latest", "newest", "current", "today": with them, all three models looked things up in every run. Without them, the model mostly answers from memory.

Coding tasks don't trigger lookups. "Write a workflow", "write a SAM template", "write a Stripe client" all pin a version, and the model picks it from memory. Most of the stale values in this test were written into files, not stated in answers.

"How do I use this API?" is the hardest case. It doesn't sound time-sensitive, so no model checked. But SDKs change their APIs, and the answer is the old API with no warning.

Read the version pins in every diff. Actions versions, runtime identifiers, API version strings, base image tags. These are the lines most likely to come from old training data, and the easiest to check.

Put the rule in CLAUDE.md. One paragraph took version pins in coding tasks from 0 of 6 to 6 of 6 for setup-node and the Lambda runtime. It costs extra lookups on every coding task. It fixes versions reliably. It changes the approach only when the model reads beyond the version number, which Opus did and Haiku did not.

When you need the newest thing, say "newest", and name the month if it's recent. "Newest stable Python" triggered a lookup every time. "October 2026" in the query got past stale search snapshots. And if you know a feature launched last week, name it. A search built from the model's memory can only confirm that memory.

articles.title: Twitter Added id_str in 2010 Because JavaScript Can't Hold a Java long
articles.description: Twitter shipped every ID twice so JavaScript wouldn't round them. Your Spring or Ktor Long IDs hit the same wall in TypeScript, silently. The fixes.
articles.body_html:
• Book: Kotlin and Java to TypeScript
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

On October 18, 2010, Twitter told every developer on its API that tweet IDs were about to change shape. A new generator called Snowflake would produce 64-bit IDs, and TechCrunch's write-up of the notice put the date plainly: "on November 26, these IDs will go longer than 53 bits." The fix Twitter shipped was blunt. Starting October 22, every ID in a JSON response would come back twice, once as a number and once as a string. In the words of developer advocate Matt Harris, quoted in the same article: "To allow javascript and JSON parsers to read the IDs we need to include a string version of any ID."

That string field is id_str, and it is still in the API. The current X developer docs tell v1.1 clients to "always use id_str", and v2 skipped the number entirely: IDs come back as strings by default.

Sixteen years later, the same bug still ships. A Spring Boot or Ktor service returns a Long ID, a TypeScript client calls JSON.parse, and the last few digits change. No exception. No warning in the console. The client then sends the wrong ID back to the server, and you get a 404 on a record that exists, or a hit on a different record whose ID happens to be the rounded value.

Why Twitter needed 64 bits in the first place

Snowflake was built for Twitter's move from MySQL to Cassandra. The original README is direct about the motive: "there is no sequential id generation facility in Cassandra, nor should there be." The requirements were uncoordinated generation across machines, rough time ordering, and IDs that stay under 64 bits.

The layout it settled on:

  • 41 bits of millisecond timestamp against a custom epoch ("gives us 69 years")
  • 10 bits of machine ID, for up to 1024 machines
  • 12 bits of sequence number, rolling over every 4096 IDs per machine

That is 63 bits of payload, which fits a signed 64-bit integer: a Java long, a Kotlin Long, a Scala Long. The Java Language Specification gives long the range -9223372036854775808 to 9223372036854775807. Every JVM backend can hold a Snowflake ID without thinking about it. The trouble starts when the ID leaves the JVM.


A JVM long has 64 bits to spend. A JavaScript number has 53 for the integer part.

53 bits of mantissa versus 64 bits of long

A JavaScript number is an IEEE 754 double. MDN's page on Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER spells out the consequence: a double "only has 52 bits to represent the mantissa," plus one implicit leading bit, so it can only safely represent integers between -(2^53 - 1) and 2^53 - 1. That ceiling is 9007199254740991.

Past it, a double still exists for every power of two, but not for every integer. Just above 2^53 the gap between neighbouring doubles is 2. Just above 2^60 it is 2^(60-52), which is 256. Modern Snowflake IDs live up there, so a parsed ID snaps to the nearest representable double, and two real IDs generated a moment apart can land on the same one.

You can see it in four lines:

const body = '{"id": 9007199254740993}';
const order = JSON.parse(body) as { id: number };

console.log(order.id);                       // 9007199254740992
console.log(Number.isSafeInteger(order.id)); // false

MDN shows the same collapse from the arithmetic side: Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 1 === Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2 evaluates to true. The X docs use 10765432100123456789, which is past even a Java long's ceiling, and show it printing back as 10765432100123458000.

None of this breaks the JSON spec. RFC 8259, section 6 "allows implementations to set limits on the range and precision of numbers accepted," and names only the integers in [-(2^53)+1, (2^53)-1] as the range where implementations "will agree exactly on their numeric values." Jackson writing 9007199254740993 is valid JSON. JSON.parse rounding it is also valid. The contract between them is the bug.

TypeScript does not help here. JSON.parse returns any, your as { id: number } is a promise you made to the compiler, and the value already satisfies number. The type system checks the shape, and the shape is fine.

Why BigInt doesn't fix JSON.parse

The natural reaction from a JVM developer is: JavaScript has arbitrary-precision integers now, so parse into BigInt. Two things get in the way.

First, JSON.parse never produces a BigInt. Numbers become doubles during parsing, before your code sees anything. The MDN JSON.parse page is explicit that the reviver "is run after the value is parsed," so numbers "will have already been converted to JavaScript numbers, and may lose precision in the process." Writing BigInt(value) inside a classic two-argument reviver gives you an exact BigInt of the wrong number.

Second, the trip back is closed by default. Per MDN's BigInt page, calling JSON.stringify() on any value containing a BigInt throws a TypeError unless you supply a toJSON or a replacer.

So BigInt is a fine type to hold an ID once you have the exact digits. It cannot recover digits the parser already threw away. The digits have to survive the parse, which means either they arrive as a string, or the parser hands you the source text.


Above 2^53, distinct IDs can parse to the same JavaScript number.

Fix it on the JVM side: make the ID a string in the contract

The fix Twitter chose, and the one Discord documents for its own Snowflake IDs ("they are always returned as strings in the HTTP API"), is to put the ID on the wire as a JSON string. Keep Long in the database and in your domain model. Change only the serialized form.

With Jackson, a per-field annotation does it:

import com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonFormat;

public record OrderDto(
    @JsonFormat(shape = JsonFormat.Shape.STRING)
    long id,
    long totalCents
) {}

In Jackson 2, the number serializers return ToStringSerializer.instance when the shape is STRING, so id goes out as "9007199254740993" with the quotes. The annotation lives in jackson-annotations, which the Spring team notes kept its package unchanged when Spring Boot 4 moved to Jackson 3 under tools.jackson, so the same line works across that upgrade.

If every Long in your API is an identifier, you can register the serializer by type instead. On Spring Boot 3 with Jackson 2:

@Bean
Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer longsAsStrings() {
    return b -> b
        .serializerByType(Long.class, ToStringSerializer.instance)
        .serializerByType(Long.TYPE, ToStringSerializer.instance);
}

Be careful with that one. It also quotes counts, cents and timestamps that never needed it. Jackson's blunter switch, JsonWriteFeature.WRITE_NUMBERS_AS_STRINGS (off by default), "forces all regular number values to be written as JSON Strings," doubles included. Per field is usually the honest scope.

On Ktor with kotlinx.serialization, the library ships a serializer for exactly this case. The LongAsStringSerializer docs describe it as "intended to be used for interoperability with external clients (mainly JavaScript ones)":

import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable
import kotlinx.serialization.builtins.LongAsStringSerializer

@Serializable
data class OrderDto(
    @Serializable(with = LongAsStringSerializer::class)
    val id: Long,
    val totalCents: Long,
)

Then write it down. If you publish an OpenAPI spec, the ID is type: string, not type: integer, format: int64, so generated TypeScript clients get string too.

Fix it in the TypeScript client

On the client, type the ID as what it is on the wire: a string. A branded type keeps it from mixing with other strings:

type OrderId = string & { readonly __brand: "OrderId" };

interface Order {
  id: OrderId;
  totalCents: number;
}

You compare it, put it in URLs and send it back. You almost never do arithmetic on an ID, so a string loses nothing. If you need ordering or math, convert with BigInt(order.id) at that moment, from exact digits.

Sometimes you don't own the server and it still sends bare numbers. For that case, TC39 added source text access to JSON.parse; the proposal is at stage 4. For primitive values, the reviver gets a third context argument whose source property is "the original JSON string representing this value" (MDN). MDN's compatibility data lists it in Chrome 114, Firefox 135, Safari 18.4, Node.js 21, Deno 1.33 and Bun 1.1.43.

type Ctx = { source?: string };

function idsAsStrings(key: string, value: unknown, ctx?: Ctx) {
  if (key !== "id" || typeof value !== "number") return value;
  if (ctx?.source === undefined) {
    throw new Error("JSON.parse source access not supported");
  }
  return ctx.source; // the exact digits, before rounding
}

const order = JSON.parse(text, idsAsStrings) as Order;

The reviver throws when the runtime doesn't pass context, because falling back to String(value) would hand you the rounded digits as a string, which is the original bug wearing a disguise. And you need the raw text to call it: Response.json() takes no reviver, so read the body with await res.text() and parse it yourself.

The same proposal added JSON.rawJSON for the outbound direction. A replacer like typeof v === "bigint" ? JSON.rawJSON(v.toString()) : v lets JSON.stringify emit a BigInt as a bare JSON number without precision loss, when a server insists on numeric IDs in request bodies.

If you own the server, the one-line @JsonFormat change is the whole fix, and it costs less to ship before your ID generator crosses 2^53 than after the first 404 on a record that exists.

If this was useful

This bug lives exactly on the seam between the JVM and TypeScript: a Long that is perfectly safe on one side and quietly lossy on the other. Kotlin and Java to TypeScript is the book I wrote for that seam, mapping what you already know from Java and Kotlin (variance, null safety, sealed hierarchies, coroutines) onto how TypeScript does the same jobs.

It's part of The TypeScript Library, five books with a clear path through them. Books 1 and 2 are the core path. If you come from the JVM, book 3 stands in for book 1. If you ship TypeScript at work, book 5 is the production layer:

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

articles.title: CrumbDesk: AI Can Read the Cake Order. It Doesn’t Get to Run the Bakery
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle.          ...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle.

What I Built

A customer orders a 500g cake. The baker accepts it, buys ingredients, and starts preparing it.

Then a message arrives: “Can we make that 1kg instead?”

An AI model can understand that message. The difficult question is what happens next.

A larger cake can affect ingredient quantities, preparation time, packaging, price, and other orders already promised. Quietly changing 500g to 1kg would erase the decision that matters.

That is why I built CrumbDesk: a local-first AI order-management tool for independent home bakers and small cottage bakeries.

CrumbDesk turns manually copied customer messages into structured, reviewable order details using Gemma 3 4B through local Ollama inference. It helps surface missing details, draft clarification replies, record change proposals, and preserve the baker’s authority over accepted orders.

The principle behind the project is simple:

Let the model interpret the message. Let deterministic code enforce the rules. Let the baker make the decision.

Home bakers often manage orders through WhatsApp, Instagram, SMS, and calls. A single message can mix flavour, quantity, weight, dietary preference, pickup time, payment statements, and special notes. Once more chats arrive, those details become difficult to find and easy to overlook.

CrumbDesk gives those details one dedicated workspace: orders needing review, confirmed orders, upcoming fulfilments, filters, local model status, and CSV export.

CrumbDesk’s dashboard gives the baker one local view of order status, schedules, and payment context.

The workflow starts with a deliberate boundary: the baker copies a customer message into CrumbDesk. The app does not automatically read WhatsApp or Instagram messages.

The baker pastes an informal customer message and requests structured extraction with local Gemma 3 4B.

Gemma helps identify the product, quantity, weight, date, time, dietary preference, fulfilment method, notes, and payment context. But its output is only a draft, never an accepted order.

For example, “Sunday” is not silently converted into a specific calendar date without enough information. “I paid via GPay” is recorded as a customer-reported claim, not proof that money cleared in a bank account. And one cake remains separate from one kilogram.

The review panel keeps extracted information editable and flags details that need baker clarification before confirmation.

If information is missing, CrumbDesk can generate an editable reply draft for the baker to copy into their chat app. This is intentionally deterministic: it uses known missing details instead of asking the model to make another unnecessary decision.

CrumbDesk prepares a polite, editable clarification reply without sending a message automatically.

Demo

The demo shows the complete flow: importing a customer message, reviewing the extracted order, confirming it, recording a later change request, and preserving the result in the order history.

Watch the CrumbDesk demo on YouTube

Code

The project is available here:

CrumbDesk on GitHub

CrumbDesk is built with Next.js and TypeScript, local Ollama inference, validation and order-management logic, browser storage, and automated tests.

How I Built It

The AI path is intentionally narrow.

A baker pastes a message into CrumbDesk, and a Next.js route sends it to Gemma 3 4B running locally through Ollama. The model returns structured order data, which is then parsed, normalized, and reviewed before the baker confirms anything.

The important work happens around the model output.

CrumbDesk validates the distinction between quantity and weight, preserves unresolved date wording rather than guessing, and prevents payment claims from becoming payment verification. A model can extract plausible information, but it cannot know whether a baker is available, whether “Sunday” means the intended date, or whether a payment has actually cleared.

Once an order is confirmed, its important details are protected. A customer change becomes a proposal, not a silent edit. The baker sees a field-level comparison and chooses whether to approve or reject it.

The requested change from 500g to 1kg is visible as a proposal, while the accepted order remains protected.

The change policy is enforced by deterministic application logic. CrumbDesk calculates a deadline only when a fulfilment date and time are resolved. Once preparation starts, ordinary changes are locked. Older proposals cannot overwrite newer accepted information.

A late or in-preparation request can still be considered, but it must be treated as an exception. The baker must deliberately approve it, provide a meaningful reason, and acknowledge the production risk.

Late changes require deliberate exception approval, a written reason, and clear acknowledgement of the production risk.

Every important action is recorded locally: creation, confirmation, change requests, decisions, and field differences. The history is not a cryptographic ledger; it is an operational record that helps the baker understand what changed and why. Orders can also be exported as CSV for kitchen preparation or record-keeping.

The order history preserves the journey from creation to confirmation and change request.

Finally, the baker can configure the change cutoff. The policy is visible rather than buried inside a prompt, making the workflow inspectable and adaptable.

The policy screen makes change cutoffs, preparation locks, local inference status, and baker approval rules visible.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

CrumbDesk uses Gemma 3 4B through Ollama because local, open-weight inference is a practical fit for this workflow.

Customer messages can contain personal details, delivery information, dietary requirements, and payment claims. A local inference path means CrumbDesk does not need a hosted AI API for extraction. It also keeps the prompt, validation rules, and post-processing logic inspectable and adaptable.

Open-weight models give builders room to specialize a workflow without committing the whole product to one remote AI vendor. The model can be replaced or adjusted later, while the deterministic safeguards remain visible and testable.

Local inference has trade-offs. It requires compatible hardware, Ollama installation, and a running local model. Performance depends on the machine. Browser storage still needs backups. Local inference also does not guarantee perfect extraction, absolute privacy, or universal offline operation.

The point is not that local AI is always better. It is that, for this use case, the model can assist without becoming an unaccountable decision-maker.

Who Would Pay for This?

CrumbDesk is intended for independent home bakers and small cottage bakeries handling custom orders through informal chats.

Today, a baker may rely on chat search, notebooks, spreadsheets, or tools designed for much larger businesses. A focused product could be valuable if it reduces missed details, makes accepted commitments easier to inspect, and prevents confusing last-minute changes.

A modest subscription, paid local setup, or customization service could be a possible business model. That is a hypothesis, not a proven outcome.

CrumbDesk does not yet have verified paying customers, revenue, or a completed commercial bakery pilot. Representative test messages and community conversations are useful design signals, but they do not establish commercial demand.

The project currently has 67 passing automated Vitest tests, plus successful TypeScript and production-build checks. The repository also contains seven live Gemma/Ollama integration cases, but they were not successfully run in the latest environment because no local app was reachable.

CrumbDesk is an honest prototype with a specific idea: AI can make a messy order easier to understand, but the person responsible for the kitchen should remain responsible for the decision.

AI can read the cake order. It does not get to run the bakery.

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma

CrumbDesk uses Gemma 3 4B through local Ollama inference to turn informal customer messages into structured order details. By combining the model with deterministic validation, order-change policies, and human review, the project demonstrates how open-weight AI can support a real-world workflow without taking control away from the person running the business.

articles.title: Node 26 Ships Temporal by Default. A Carbon User's Guide to Dates in TypeScript
articles.description: Node 26 runs Temporal, no flag. Your daily Carbon and DateTimeImmutable habits beside their TypeScript twins, plus two PHP reflexes that break.
articles.body_html:
• Book: PHP to TypeScript
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

You write new Date(2026, 9, 25) for September 25 in your first Node service and get October 25, because the Date constructor counts months from zero. Then you add a day by calling setDate(), which changes the object in place, in whatever time zone the server happens to run in. If you came from PHP with Carbon in your fingers, this is the moment you start missing it.

You can stop missing it. Temporal reached Stage 4 at TC39's 113th plenary in March 2026, and Node.js 26.0.0, released on 2026-05-05, turns it on by default. No flag, no polyfill. Node 26 is still the "Current" line today, and the Node.js release schedule plans its move to Active LTS for 2026-10-28, a common point for teams to upgrade.

Almost every Carbon habit has a direct Temporal twin. Two of your reflexes don't, and they get their own section at the end. Below, each PHP snippet sits next to the TypeScript that does the same job. Run the PHP with php and the TypeScript with node.

Setup: Node 26 and a small tsconfig

Node 26 runs .ts files directly. Type stripping has been on by default since v23.6.0 and stable since v25.2.0, so node dates.ts works as long as you stick to erasable syntax (no enum, no parameter properties). Node does no type checking at run time; your editor and tsc do.

For the types, TypeScript 6.0 ships built-in Temporal declarations. Enable them with esnext or the narrower esnext.temporal lib. The same release changes the default types to [], so @types/node (and with it console) is no longer picked up on its own. Install it with npm i -D @types/node and list it:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2024",
    "lib": ["es2024", "esnext.temporal"],
    "types": ["node"],
    "module": "nodenext",
    "noEmit": true,
    "erasableSyntaxOnly": true
  }
}

erasableSyntaxOnly makes tsc reject the syntax Node can't strip, so the "no enum" rule is enforced for you.

On the PHP side, the snippets use the built-in DateTimeImmutable and Carbon 3 (composer require nesbot/carbon). If you are still on Node 24, the @js-temporal/polyfill package provides the same API, with two caveats: it does not install a global, so add import { Temporal } from '@js-temporal/polyfill'; at the top of each file, and its README still marks it as not yet production-ready.

PlainDate: the type PHP never gave you

PHP has no date-only type. new DateTimeImmutable('2026-10-15') is midnight in your default time zone, and Carbon extends DateTime, so it carries the same baggage. Temporal splits the concepts: PlainDate is a calendar date with no time and no zone, which is what a birthday, an invoice due date or a holiday actually is.

<?php
$d = new DateTimeImmutable('2026-10-15');
$next = $d->modify('+1 day');
echo $d->format('Y-m-d'), ' ', $next->format('Y-m-d'), PHP_EOL;
// 2026-10-15 2026-10-16

const d = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-10-15');
const next = d.add({ days: 1 });
console.log(d.toString(), next.toString());
// 2026-10-15 2026-10-16

Month ends are where the two part ways. PHP lets day numbers overflow into the next month: "2008-06-31" means July 1. So January 31 plus one month becomes February 31, which rolls over to March 3 in 2026. Temporal's default is to clamp to the last valid day instead.

<?php
$jan = new DateTimeImmutable('2026-01-31');
echo $jan->modify('+1 month')->format('Y-m-d'), PHP_EOL;
// 2026-03-03

const jan = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-01-31');
console.log(jan.add({ months: 1 }).toString());
// 2026-02-28

Pass { overflow: 'reject' } as the second argument and Temporal throws a RangeError rather than clamping. from() takes the same option, and that is the one you want for anything a user typed.

Parsing is the other big difference. createFromFormat() has no Temporal twin: PlainDate.from() takes RFC 9557 strings (ISO-style 2026-10-15) or an object. For a d/m/Y string, split it yourself and hand Temporal the parts:

<?php
$utc = new DateTimeZone('UTC');
$d = DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat(
    '!d/m/Y', '15/10/2026', $utc
);
echo $d->format('Y-m-d'), PHP_EOL; // 2026-10-15

function fromDmy(s: string): Temporal.PlainDate {
  const [day, month, year] = s.split('/').map(Number);
  return Temporal.PlainDate.from(
    { year, month, day },
    { overflow: 'reject' },
  );
}
console.log(fromDmy('15/10/2026').toString()); // 2026-10-15

Note the ! in the PHP format. Without it, every field you don't parse is filled from the current system time, so your "date" quietly carries the time the request ran. A PlainDate has no time to leak.


PlainDate is a date with the clock and the time zone removed.

ZonedDateTime and the 25-hour Sunday

In 2026, Europe falls back on Sunday, October 25, and the US on Sunday, November 1. That makes October 25 in Berlin a 25-hour day, and it is the classic place where "add one day" and "add 24 hours" stop meaning the same thing.

PHP has both behaviours, spread across two methods that look alike: modify('+1 day') keeps the wall-clock time, while add(new DateInterval('PT24H')) adds elapsed time. The PHP manual's arithmetic examples walk through the same split between modify() and add():

<?php
$tz = new DateTimeZone('Europe/Berlin');
$sat = new DateTimeImmutable('2026-10-24 12:00', $tz);
echo $sat->modify('+1 day')->format('c'), PHP_EOL;
// 2026-10-25T12:00:00+01:00
echo $sat->add(new DateInterval('PT24H'))->format('c'), PHP_EOL;
// 2026-10-25T11:00:00+01:00

Temporal has one rule, and it is easy to remember. Days use calendar arithmetic and keep the clock time; hours use exact elapsed time:

const sat = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from(
  '2026-10-24T12:00[Europe/Berlin]',
);
const sun = sat.add({ days: 1 });
console.log(sun.toString());
// 2026-10-25T12:00:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]
console.log(sat.add({ hours: 24 }).toString());
// 2026-10-25T11:00:00+01:00[Europe/Berlin]
console.log(sun.hoursInDay); // 25

The zone lives inside the value as a bracketed IANA name, so the result never depends on what TZ the container was started with. hoursInDay is a nice bonus for billing or shift code that needs to know how long "today" is.

Time zone conversion is setTimezone() in PHP and withTimeZone() in Temporal. Both keep the instant and change the zone:

<?php
$berlin = new DateTimeImmutable(
    '2026-10-15 18:00', new DateTimeZone('Europe/Berlin')
);
$ny = $berlin->setTimezone(new DateTimeZone('America/New_York'));
echo $ny->format('c'), PHP_EOL;
// 2026-10-15T12:00:00-04:00

const berlin = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from(
  '2026-10-15T18:00[Europe/Berlin]',
);
const ny = berlin.withTimeZone('America/New_York');
console.log(ny.toString());
// 2026-10-15T12:00:00-04:00[America/New_York]

const later = berlin.add({ days: 11 });
console.log(later.withTimeZone('America/New_York').toString());
// 2026-10-26T13:00:00-04:00[America/New_York]

The second result is the week between the two fall-backs: Berlin is already on winter time, New York is not, so your 18:00 call lands at 13:00 instead of 12:00. Temporal gets that right because it keeps the real zone, not a fixed offset.

Durations and diffInDays

PHP's DateInterval and Temporal's Duration read the same ISO 8601 strings, so PT1H30M means the same thing in both. The difference is that Duration can total itself:

<?php
$i = new DateInterval('PT1H30M');
echo $i->h * 60 + $i->i, PHP_EOL; // 90

const dur = Temporal.Duration.from('PT1H30M');
console.log(dur.total({ unit: 'minutes' })); // 90

For "how many days between", PHP gives you DateInterval::$days, which is non-negative, with the direction in $invert. Carbon 3 changed its version: diffIn* methods now return a float and are signed by default ($absolute = false). If your code was written against Carbon 2, that is worth a grep.

<?php
require 'vendor/autoload.php';
use Carbon\CarbonImmutable;

$a = CarbonImmutable::parse('2026-10-15', 'UTC');
$b = CarbonImmutable::parse('2026-12-25', 'UTC');
var_dump($a->diffInDays($b)); // float(71)
var_dump($b->diffInDays($a)); // float(-71)

Temporal's until() and since() return a Duration, signed, and for a PlainDate the largest unit defaults to days:

const a = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-10-15');
const b = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-12-25');
console.log(a.until(b).days); // 71
console.log(b.until(a).days); // -71
const parts = a.until(b, { largestUnit: 'months' });
console.log(parts.toString()); // P2M10D

Integer days, no float to cast, and no time zone to pin to UTC first, because a PlainDate doesn't have one.

The two PHP habits that bite

Habit one: expecting a call to change the object. Carbon is mutable. A Carbon modifier changes and returns the same instance, which is the source of the classic "why did my start date move" bug:

<?php
require 'vendor/autoload.php';
use Carbon\Carbon;

$start = Carbon::parse('2026-10-15');
$end = $start->addDays(7);
echo $start->toDateString(), PHP_EOL; // 2026-10-22
var_dump($start === $end);            // bool(true)

Every Temporal type is immutable, so the bug flips direction. If you call add() as a statement, the way you would on mutable Carbon, the result goes nowhere and nothing changes. TypeScript won't warn you about a discarded return value:

const start = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-10-15');
start.add({ days: 7 });            // result thrown away
console.log(start.toString());     // 2026-10-15
const end = start.add({ days: 7 });
console.log(end.toString());       // 2026-10-22
console.log(start.with({ day: 1 }).toString()); // 2026-10-01

There are no setters. with() is how you "set" a field, and it returns a new value too. If you already use CarbonImmutable or DateTimeImmutable, you have the right reflex: always assign the result.

Habit two: comparing with operators. PHP compares DateTime objects by value with ==, < and >, and === checks identity:

<?php
$a = new DateTimeImmutable('2026-10-25');
$b = new DateTimeImmutable('2026-10-25');
var_dump($a == $b);  // bool(true)
var_dump($a === $b); // bool(false)
var_dump($a < $b);   // bool(false)

JavaScript has no value-equality operator for objects. === is identity, so two equal dates built separately are not ===. And < doesn't silently compare strings: Temporal's valueOf() always throws a TypeError so the mistake fails loudly.

const a = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-10-25');
const b = Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-10-25');
console.log(a === b);      // false: two objects
console.log(a.equals(b));  // true
console.log(Temporal.PlainDate.compare(a, b)); // 0
// a < b throws TypeError: valueOf() always throws

const dates = [b, Temporal.PlainDate.from('2026-01-01')];
dates.sort(Temporal.PlainDate.compare);
const unique = new Set(dates.map(String));
console.log([...unique]); // [ '2026-01-01', '2026-10-25' ]

compare slots straight into sort(). For Set or Map keys, convert to strings first, because the Set holds objects by identity.


Two equal values, two separate objects: === sees the objects, equals() sees the values.

One trap inside the trap: for ZonedDateTime, equals() checks the instant, the time zone and the calendar, while ZonedDateTime.compare() looks only at the instant. The same moment in Berlin and New York is compare() === 0 but not equals(). In practice, PHP's == on two zoned DateTime values compares the instant, like compare(), so when you port an equality check, decide which question you were asking.

If this was useful

The date API is a small slice of the PHP-to-TypeScript move. The bigger shifts (sync to async, structural typing, unions where you used to reach for class hierarchies) are what PHP to TypeScript is about, written for PHP 8+ developers who already know how to build things and want the mapping, not a beginner course.

It is book 4 of The TypeScript Library. If you came from PHP, start with PHP to TypeScript; add The TypeScript Type System once the basics stick, and TypeScript in Production when you are shipping at work:

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

articles.title: The One-Line Package That Broke create-react-app
articles.description: A tiny npm library shipped a "minor" release and broke some of the biggest JavaScript tools for three hours. What it teaches every backend engineer about Semantic Versioning.
articles.body_html:
Minor Release, Major Damage

Here is the entire job of a package called is-promise:

function isPromise(obj) {
  return !!obj && (typeof obj === 'object' || typeof obj === 'function')
    && typeof obj.then === 'function';
}

One function. It checks whether something looks like a Promise.

That's it.

In April 2020, it was being downloaded around 12 million times a week. GitHub counted about 3.5 million projects depending on it, mostly without knowing it existed.

On Saturday, 25 April 2020, its maintainer published version 2.2.0.

Within hours, people trying to start a new project with create-react-app, angular-cli or firebase-tools were staring at an error instead.

The version number said minor. Nothing about the result was minor.

What the Version Number Promised

Semantic Versioning gives every release three numbers: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.

  • PATCH means a bug fix. Nothing new, nothing removed.
  • MINOR means something new was added, and everything that worked before still works.
  • MAJOR means something changed in a way that can break you. Read the notes before upgrading.

That promise is what makes automatic upgrades possible. When a project lists a dependency as "is-promise": "^2.1.0", the caret says: give me any 2.x version from 2.1.0 upward. Patches and minors flow in on their own, because SemVer says they're safe.

Python works the same way. requests~=2.31 or django>=5.0,<6.0 in your requirements are the same bet: anything below the next MAJOR shouldn't break you.

So when 2.2.0 appeared, thousands of dependency trees picked it up with nobody clicking anything.

That's the system working exactly as designed. It's also why a mislabelled release spreads so fast.

What Actually Changed

Version 2.2.0 was the first release of is-promise in about five years. The maintainer, Forbes Lindesay, wanted to modernise it: add support for ES Modules, JavaScript's newer import system, while keeping the old CommonJS require() working.

The changes were small and reasonable:

  • A default export, so modern code could import isPromise from 'is-promise'.
  • An exports field in package.json, the newer way of telling Node which file to load for which module system.
  • Updated TypeScript definitions.

To the author, this was an addition. New way to import it, old way still there. That's the textbook definition of MINOR.

The problem was one line in package.json. The exports field pointed to "index.js" instead of the format Node expects, a path starting with ./. Node rejected it outright:

Error [ERR_INVALID_PACKAGE_TARGET]: Invalid "exports" main target "index.js"
defined in the package config
  • It only failed on newer Node. Versions from 12.16 onward had started reading the exports field by default. Older Node ignored it, which is probably why it worked on the author's machine.
  • Lockfiles didn't save anyone. Many reports came from people running npx create-react-app. Tools run through npx install fresh, and a library's lockfile isn't used when someone else installs it. Every new project got 2.2.0.
  • One tiny package sat deep in big trees. Nobody chose is-promise. It came in through a dependency of a dependency.

The maintainer moved fast. Around three hours later, version 2.2.2 was out, and it simply dropped the ES Module support. The modern version eventually shipped properly, as a new MAJOR release: 4.0.0.

The Question That Would Have Caught It

Here's the detail I find most interesting.

Node's own documentation on dual-module packages already said that adding exports and type to an existing package is a breaking change. Even when done perfectly, the exports field changes which files consumers are allowed to load. Anyone who imported a deep path like is-promise/index.js could break even with a correct config.

So the honest version number was 3.0.0, before the typo was even made.

The author labelled the release by intent: I'm adding a feature. SemVer asks about impact: what will your users notice?

Those are different questions, and they give different answers more often than we admit.

The question I use now, for libraries and for APIs, is:

"Can anyone using this observe the difference?"

Not "did I mean to break something." Not "is this technically a feature." Just whether someone on the other side could notice.

The Same Trap in Your Backend

You don't need to publish npm packages to fall into this. Every backend API has consumers, and the same gap between intent and impact shows up in ordinary tickets:

  • Tightening validation. You add a minimum length on a username field. It feels like an addition. But a request that returned 200 yesterday returns 400 today. You removed something.
  • Fixing a value. Your API returned status labels in the wrong language, and you fix it. Any client that matched on the old strings now breaks. With enough users, someone depends on every observable behaviour, bugs included. That idea even has a name: Hyrum's Law.
  • Correcting a calculation. Same field, same type, different number. If clients make decisions on it, their decisions just changed without warning.
  • Adding a field. Usually safe. Not for clients with strict schema validation that rejects unknown fields.

Here's the decision tree I'd put in a pull request template:

Can any consumer observe the difference?
│
├── NO  → PATCH (internal fixes, performance, logging)
│
└── YES → What kind of difference?
          ├── Removes, renames, or changes a type        → MAJOR
          ├── Rejects input that used to be accepted     → MAJOR
          ├── Changes how the package/API is loaded      → MAJOR
          ├── Changes the meaning of an existing output  → MAJOR, or MINOR with advance notice
          └── Adds something optional                    → MINOR

The is-promise change sits on the third branch. It changed how the package was loaded, which is exactly why it needed a new MAJOR.

When a Patch Really Is a Patch

None of this means every release should be MAJOR.

A slow query made faster is a patch. An internal log nobody else can see is a patch. A crash fixed in a code path that never returned anything useful is a patch.

And inflating versions has its own cost. If every release is "breaking," consumers stop reading the number and pin everything forever. Then they miss your security fixes too.

The version only works as a signal if it's honest in both directions.

"It's only a small change" isn't evidence. "It works on my machine" definitely isn't.

What the Maintainer Did Next

The best part of this story is how it was handled.

Forbes Lindesay shipped a fix within hours and wrote a public post-mortem. He added end-to-end tests that install the package the way a real user would, then check it actually loads. And the ES Module support came back later as a proper major version instead of a minor.

It was an honest mistake that could have happened to almost anyone. What's worth copying is the response: test from the consumer's side, and let the version number tell the truth.

The Real Lesson

Semantic Versioning looks like it's about code. It's really a promise to the people who depend on you, written in three numbers.

is-promise didn't break because it was small, or because one-line packages are silly. It broke because the version described what the author meant to do, while millions of installs depended on what the release actually did.

Before you pick the next version number, ask one question:

"Can anyone tell the difference?"

If they can, the PATCH or MINOR has to justify itself.

Your turn 👇

What's the smallest release you've seen break something big? I'd like to hear the gray-zone stories other engineers have run into. Share yours in the comments.

If this was useful, follow me here for more stories from the backend trenches, and subscribe to The Backend Tech Lead on Substack for weekly blueprints.
